lead: Mood disorders that start in the puerperium or the months after birth, from a mild self-limited low mood to a psychiatric emergency: baby blues (50–80%), postnatal depression (10–15%), puerperal psychosis (1–2 per 1000).
f: The three compared

Blues: day 3–10, peak day 4–5, gone by 2 wk; tearful, labile; still cares for the baby; insight full · Depression: usually by 3 months, lasts months; anhedonia, guilt, poor bonding; insight present · Psychosis: first 2 weeks, sudden; mania or mixed, delusions, confusion; insight lost; suicide and infanticide risk

sc: Day 4, cries easily, feeds the baby well → Baby blues: reassure
Day 5, no sleep, says the baby is evil → Puerperal psychosis

f: Aetiology
Sudden fall of oestrogen and progesterone after the placenta, plus sleep loss, pain and stress · Psychosis is mostly a bipolar episode triggered by delivery
Baby blues
Up to 80% · Explain, rest, family support · Review if it lasts > 2 weeks: severe or long blues is a risk factor for depression

tr: Do not start an antidepressant for blues on day 4; still present at 3 weeks → screen for depression

f: Physical illness that mimics a mood disorder

Sepsis delirium and malaria · eclampsia, stroke · cerebral vein thrombosis (headache, fits, normal BP) · anaemia · postpartum thyroiditis (hypo phase at 4–8 months) · Sheehan syndrome · drugs, glucose, sodium

sc: Day 5, confused, temperature 39 °C → Exclude sepsis and malaria first
5 months, low mood, cold, weight gain → Postpartum thyroiditis

f: Postnatal depression

Within the first year, usually by 3 months · Risk factors: past depression or PND, depression in pregnancy, severe blues, poor support, marital conflict, sick baby or stillbirth · Features ≥ 2 weeks: low mood, anhedonia, insomnia even when the baby sleeps, guilt ("bad mother"), suicidal thoughts; mothers hide it
Screening
EPDS: 10 questions, 0–3 each, at booking and 6 wk · ≥ 13 = probable depression · Any score on question 10 (self-harm) → same-day assessment · Check Hb and TSH
Management of depression

Mild: support, CBT, review 2–4 wk · Moderate–severe: sertraline 50 mg daily (to 200 mg) + CBT; continue 6 months after recovery · Suicidal or psychotic: admit · Keep breastfeeding; avoid fluoxetine (builds up in the baby) · Effect on the infant: poor bonding, growth, later behaviour

sc: Breastfeeding mother, 7 wk, moderate depression → Sertraline; continue breastfeeding

f: Puerperal psychosis

Onset within 2–4 weeks, often after nights without sleep · Agitated, confused, rapidly changing mood, delusions about the baby, hallucinations; unaware she is ill · Risk factors: previous puerperal psychosis, bipolar disorder, family history, primigravida, stopping a mood stabiliser
Management of psychosis: an emergency

Never leave her alone with the baby · Same-day psychiatry; admit, ideally a mother-and-baby unit · Exclude organic causes · Olanzapine or haloperidol; lithium for mania · ECT if life-threatening or not eating · Breastfeeding usually possible on antipsychotics; not on lithium

sc: Hears voices telling her the baby is the devil → Do not leave her alone; urgent psychiatry, admit
tr: Psychosis is not "severe blues": never send her home with reassurance

f: Drugs in pregnancy and breastfeeding

Sertraline: SSRI of choice after birth · Paroxetine: fine in breastfeeding, avoid in early pregnancy (heart defects) · Fluoxetine: long half-life, not first choice · Lithium: Ebstein anomaly; high in milk → bottle-feed · Valproate: avoid in women who may conceive (neural tube defects, low IQ)
Prevention and recurrence

Ask every woman at booking about past depression, psychosis, bipolar, family history · Bipolar: switch valproate before pregnancy, shared plan, prophylaxis right after birth · Recurrence: PND about 25% next birth · psychosis about 50% · bipolar with past or family puerperal psychosis about 60%

sc: Postnatal depression last time → About 1 in 4 recurrence
